definition: An organic compound whose molecules carry the hydroxyl (–OH) functional group covalently bonded to a carbon chain. A homologous series, not a single substance.
msAccepts: OH bonded to a carbon chain

definition: The atom or bond arrangement that gives an organic family its characteristic reactions. For the alcohols it is the –OH group; for the alkenes it was C=C.
msAccepts: the reactive part determining chemical properties
msAvoids: giving C=C as the alcohol group

definition: A family of compounds with the same functional group, similar chemical properties, a trend in physical properties, one general formula, and consecutive members differing by a -CH2- unit.
msAvoids: listing bullets without the functional-group thread

definition: The alcohol CH3CH2OH (molecular formula C2H6O): the 'alcohol' of everyday speech, the family's representative, and the product of both industrial routes.
msAccepts: the alcohol in drinks properly called ethanol
msAvoids: calling ethanol 'alcohol' as if it were the only member
writing C2H6O only when the structure is asked

definition: The simplest alcohol, CH3OH (molecular formula CH4O): one carbon bearing the –OH group. First member of the series.
msAvoids: omitting the O from the formula

definition: A formula counting the atoms of each element in one molecule — C2H6O for ethanol — without showing how they are joined.
msAccepts: shows what but not how joined
msAvoids: omitting the O in alcohol formulae

definition: A drawing showing every atom and every bond as an explicit line. For alcohols the O–H bond must be shown — an oxygen with no H drawn is the classic lost mark.
A compound with the same molecular formula as another but a different structure. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are isomers: the –OH sits on a different carbon.
msAccepts: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol as an isomer pair
msAvoids: treating the locant as a drawing convention only

definition: Burning in plenty of oxygen. Ethanol burns to carbon dioxide and water only: C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l).
msAvoids: listing CO or soot for complete combustion
wrong state symbols for ethanol (it is a liquid)

definition: A fuel made from biological sources, such as sugar cane or corn, rather than from fossil crude oil. Ethanol used in petrol mixtures in Brazil is the standard example.
msAccepts: made from sugar cane or corn
msAvoids: saying biofuels burn to different products
confusing renewability with different combustion chemistry

definition: Oxidation of ethanol by oxygen in the air with the help of microorganisms (bacteria or yeast), forming ethanoic acid — the wine-turns-to-vinegar reaction.
msAccepts: reaction with oxygen in the air (microbial oxidation)
msAvoids: saying direct air oxidation needs no living help

definition: The carboxylic acid CH3COOH, the product of all three ethanol oxidations. Old name: acetic acid. Member of the carboxylic acid family.
The substance that oxidises another by taking electrons from it. In the lab oxidation of ethanol: potassium dichromate(VI) plus dilute sulfuric acid, written [O] in equations.
msAccepts: potassium dichromate(VI) with dilute sulfuric acid
msAvoids: omitting the acid from the reagent pair

definition: Heating with a condenser placed vertically so vapours condense and run back into the flask instead of escaping — keeps volatile reactants in the reaction.
msAccepts: condenser vertical, vapours condensed and returned
heat under reflux keeps volatile ethanol in

definition: Yeast enzymes converting sugar (glucose) into ethanol and carbon dioxide, in the absence of air at about 30 degrees C: C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2.
msAccepts: enzymes in yeast convert glucose to ethanol + CO2
msAvoids: naming pure ethanol as the product

definition: The sugar C6H12O6 that yeast enzymes convert into ethanol and carbon dioxide during fermentation; obtained from sugar cane, maize (corn), wheat and other starchy materials.
A biological catalyst — a protein — that speeds a reaction without being consumed. Yeast enzymes convert sugar to ethanol; they denature above about 40 degrees C.
msAvoids: calling it a chemical catalyst like phosphoric acid

definition: The microorganism whose enzymes carry out fermentation; supplies the biological catalysts, is killed above about 15% alcohol, and works only in the absence of air for ethanol production.
msAvoids: saying yeast is the catalyst itself (its enzymes are)

definition: In the absence of air. Fermentation must be anaerobic: with air (aerobic conditions), yeast enzymes produce carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol.
msAccepts: aerobic conditions give CO2 + water instead

definition: The addition of water (steam) across a double bond: ethene plus steam makes ethanol at ~300 degrees C, ~60-70 atm, over a phosphoric acid catalyst.
A substance that speeds a reaction without being consumed. Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) catalyses ethene hydration; enzymes catalyse fermentation.
msAvoids: swapping the two catalysts between routes

definition: A process run in discrete lots: everything is mixed in a vessel, left (for fermentation, several days), then removed and a new batch set up. Inefficient but simple.
A process where a stream of reactants constantly flows over the catalyst without stopping — more efficient than a batch process. Ethene hydration runs this way.
Separation of a liquid mixture using boiling-point differences. Needed after fermentation because yeast dies above ~15% alcohol: ethanol (78 degrees C) separates from water (100 degrees C).
msAvoids: saying fermentation alone gives pure ethanol
